questions.question: When are two norms $\|\cdot\|_p$ and $\|\cdot\|_q$ on $\boldsymbol{V}$ called equivalent?
options: When $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for all $\boldsymbol{v}$, with $a,b>0$ depending on $\boldsymbol{v}$.
When $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for some $a,b>0$ and all $\boldsymbol{v}$.
When $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for some $b>0$ and all $\boldsymbol{v}$.

questions.question: If $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q = 2\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for every $\boldsymbol{v}$, which constants show equivalence?
What is the interpretation of equivalent norms?
options: They agree on which vectors have length at most $1$.
Their ratio $\|v\|_q/\|v\|_p$ is one constant for all $v\ne0$.
Their lengths are comparable up to fixed scaling factors.
One of them is at least as large as the other for every vector.

questions.question: If $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ with $a,b \gt 0$, which reverse comparison follows?
Suppose only $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq 5\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ is known for every $\boldsymbol{v}$. Is this alone enough to prove equivalence?
options: Yes, dividing by $5$ gives the reverse bound $\frac{1}{5}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$
Yes, every norm already has the lower bound $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\geq 0$
No, because the upper constant $b=5$ would have to be at most $1$ as well
No, a lower bound $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$ with $a>0$ is also needed

questions.question: What does the lower inequality $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\le \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$ prevent?
On a finite-dimensional vector space, what can be concluded about any two norms?
options: They must both be Euclidean norms.

questions.question: If $\frac{1}{4}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\le4\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ and $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p=3$, what bounds follow for $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$?

On $\mathbb{R}^2$ consider the maximum norm $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_\infty=\max\{|v_1|,|v_2|\}$ and the Euclidean norm $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_2$. Which chain holds for every $\boldsymbol{v}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and shows the two norms are equivalent?

On the space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$, take the uniform norm $\|f\|_\infty=\max_{x\in[0,1]}|f(x)|$ and the norm $\|f\|_1=\int_0^1|f(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x$. For $f_n(x)=x^n$ one has $\|f_n\|_\infty=1$ and $\|f_n\|_1=\tfrac{1}{n+1}$. What does this show?
options: No $a>0$ satisfies $a\|f\|_\infty\le\|f\|_1$ for all $f$, so the two norms are not equivalent.
The norms are equivalent, with constants $a=\tfrac{1}{n+1}$ and $b=1$ chosen for each $f_n$.
The upper bound $\|f\|_1\le b\,\|f\|_\infty$ fails, because $\|f_n\|_1$ tends to $0$.
$\|\cdot\|_1$ is not a norm, since it assigns values tending to $0$ to functions of uniform norm $1$.

questions.question: Why do constants $a_{\boldsymbol{v}},b_{\boldsymbol{v}}>0$ that are allowed to depend on $\boldsymbol{v}$ fail to prove that two norms are equivalent?
options: For $\boldsymbol{v}\ne\boldsymbol{0}$ one can always take $a_{\boldsymbol{v}}=b_{\boldsymbol{v}}=\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q/\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$, so every pair of norms would pass.
Constants that depend on $\boldsymbol{v}$ may become negative, while equivalence needs $a,b>0$.
At $\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}$ the two bounds $a_{\boldsymbol{0}}\|\boldsymbol{0}\|_p\le\|\boldsymbol{0}\|_q\le b_{\boldsymbol{0}}\|\boldsymbol{0}\|_p$ cannot both hold.
Such $\boldsymbol{v}$-dependent constants exist only when $V$ is finite-dimensional, so they add nothing to the theorem.
